What is LFI?
LFI stands for <highlight>Local File Inclusion</highlight>. It is a vulnerability that allows an attacker to include and read files from the local server through a vulnerable parameter.

When exploiting LFI, the file is accessed by the web server process, typically running as <highlight>www-data</highlight>. This means you can only read files that the web server user (<highlight>www-data</highlight>) has permission to access.
How to Get Files Using LFI?

blocks.title: Conditions Required for LFI
items: The application must use a parameter to load or include a file.
The parameter must not properly sanitize or validate user input.
The web server must have permission to read the targeted file.

blocks.text: Now let's attempt to read a file using LFI. Below is the URL that allows us to access a file on the server.

blocks.title: Breaking Down the URL
items: The vulnerable file here is <highlight>secret-script.php</highlight>.
This file accepts a parameter that is used to include other files.
Because it does not properly validate input, we can exploit it to read files that the <highlight>web server</highlight> has access to.

blocks.text: If the exploit is successful, you will receive output similar to the following. You may also try reading <highlight>/etc/hosts</highlight> if the web server has permission to access it.
Now we will try to read the source code of the same file instead of executing it.

blocks.title: Breaking Down the Command
items: We use the <highlight>php://filter</highlight> wrapper to encode the file in <highlight>base64</highlight>.
We cannot retrieve the raw PHP source directly because it would execute on the server instead of being displayed.
After retrieving the base64-encoded content, we decode it locally to view the actual source code safely.

blocks.text: Let's examine the retrieved source code.

blocks.title: Analyzing the Source Code
items: The script checks for the parameter using <highlight>if(isset($_GET['file']))</highlight>.
There is no input validation or sanitization applied to the user-controlled parameter.
The function <highlight>include($file);</highlight> directly includes the user-supplied value, which makes this highly vulnerable to LFI.

blocks.text: Basic LFI is done here, if you really want to learn about how can we use filter wrapper then take a look at <highlight>Filter chain generator</highlight> which is using filter wrapper.
P.S: Before continuing, make sure you understand <highlight>LFI</highlight>. You can find related learning resources in the <highlight>Course Material</highlight> section.
What is a Filter Chain Generator?

blocks.title: Purpose of the Filter Chain Generator
items: The Filter Chain Generator is used to encode a PHP script so that it does not execute immediately when sent to the target machine.
It uses PHP stream <highlight>wrapper</highlight> techniques internally.
For the <highlight>Filter Chain Generator</highlight> to work, ensure that <highlight>LFI</highlight> is working on the target machine.

blocks.text: Let's look at the command used to execute the Filter Chain Generator.

blocks.title: Understanding the Command
items: It uses the <highlight>php_filter_chain_generator.py</highlight> script.
<highlight>--chain</highlight> tells the tool to encode everything that comes after it.
The PHP code provided is a one-line reverse shell that opens a connection back to the attacker.
<highlight>grep '^php'</highlight> filters the output and keeps only the line that starts with <highlight>php</highlight>.
Finally, the clean encoded payload is saved into the <highlight>payload.txt</highlight> file.

blocks.text: After this, we will send the encoded string using LFI.

blocks.title: How This Works
items: This request sends the encoded payload to the target machine through the vulnerable LFI parameter.
The <highlight>payload.txt</highlight> file contains a PHP filter chain, not just raw PHP code.
PHP will decode the chain step by step until the original PHP code is reconstructed and executed.

blocks.text: Filter - LFI

blocks.title: php://filter
items: It allows you to apply filters before PHP reads or writes a file.
In short, you are telling PHP: <highlight>Before processing this file, modify its content.</highlight>

blocks.text: Let's look at a basic example.

blocks.title: Understanding the Command
items: Here we used <highlight>convert.base64-encode</highlight> to encode the file so that PHP does not execute the code.
The server returns the content in <highlight>base64</highlight> format, which we can decode locally to read the source code.

blocks.text: Filter + read - LFI

blocks.title: What is read?
items: <highlight>read=</highlight> tells PHP to apply filters when the file is being read.
If only one filter is used, PHP assumes read mode automatically, so writing <highlight>read=</highlight> is optional.
When chaining multiple filters, <highlight>read=</highlight> must be explicitly defined.

blocks.text: Now let's look at a chained read filter.

blocks.title: Understanding the Chained Filters
items: This command first <highlight>encodes</highlight> the file using base64.
Then it applies <highlight>string.rot13</highlight> to rotate the encoded string.
Multiple filters can be combined using the <highlight>|</highlight> symbol.
Filters are applied from left to right.

blocks.text: Filter + write - LFI

blocks.title: What is write?
items: <highlight>write=</highlight> applies filters when data is being written to a file.
It modifies the data before it is saved.
This only works if the application uses file-writing functions such as <highlight>file_put_contents()</highlight> or <highlight>fwrite()</highlight>.
In a normal LFI using include(), <highlight>write=</highlight> does not work because include() only reads files.

blocks.title: Understanding the Command
items: For this to work, the application must write user-controlled data into the file.
You must supply base64-encoded content (for example in a POST body).
The write filter will decode the data first, then save the decoded result into <highlight>shell.php</highlight>.
If there is no file-writing function in the application, this technique will not work.

blocks.text: So far we have covered the two main modes supported by php://filter: read and write.

Filter Input - LFI

blocks.title: php://input
items: It is just a <highlight>PHP stream wrapper</highlight>
It contains the <highlight>raw HTTP request body</highlight>

blocks.text: Let's look at a basic example.

blocks.title: Understanding the Command
items: Here we used <highlight>php://input</highlight> which serves the raw request body.
It must be a <highlight>POST</highlight> request.
The vulnerable file must use <highlight>include()</highlight> or <highlight>require()</highlight> on user-controlled input.
Content-Type should be <highlight>text/plain</highlight> to avoid PHP consuming the body as form data.
The PHP code inside --data will only execute if <highlight>include()</highlight> processes php://input and <highlight>allow_url_include</highlight> is enabled.

blocks.text: Now let's look at the output of the above command.
Sometimes PHP stream wrappers are disabled. You need to check the configuration.
If the result shows Off, then wrapper-based RCE will not work. On real targets you cannot change this setting. On a local lab machine you can modify it for learning purposes.
Change <highlight>allow_url_include = Off</highlight> to <highlight>allow_url_include = On</highlight> and restart the PHP server.

blocks.title: LFI Practice Lab
blocks.text: Download the vulnerable PHP lab and payload collection.
We will examine each stream filter one by one.
Encoding Filters
Encodes file content into Base64 format and prevents PHP execution.
Decodes Base64 encoded content back into original form.
Encodes and then decodes the content. Final result behaves like direct file inclusion.
Encodes special characters into quoted-printable format (example: < becomes =3C).
Decodes quoted-printable encoded content back to normal text.
Converts character encoding from UTF-8 to UTF-16, modifying underlying byte structure.
Compression Filters
Compresses the file content using zlib compression.
Decompresses previously compressed zlib content.
String Filters
Applies ROT13 substitution cipher to alphabetic characters.
Converts alphabetic characters to uppercase.
Converts alphabetic characters to lowercase.
Other Filters
Removes HTTP chunked transfer encoding from content.

Data Wrapper - LFI

blocks.title: data://
items: The data:// wrapper allows embedding file content directly inside a URL.
Basic structure: <highlight>data://[mime-type],[data]</highlight>
It works when vulnerable code uses functions like <highlight>include($_GET['file']);</highlight>
<highlight>allow_url_include=On</highlight> is required when using include() with URL wrappers.
<highlight>allow_url_fopen=On</highlight> must be enabled for URL wrapper support.
If URL wrappers are disabled in php.ini, this technique will not work.

blocks.text: Execution Flow

blocks.title: How Code Executes
items: The application calls include($_GET['file']).
The data:// wrapper loads the provided content.
If base64 is specified, PHP decodes the content automatically.
The decoded content is treated as a PHP file.
Any PHP code inside executes on the server.

blocks.text: Basic execution attempt using raw payload.

blocks.code: curl: (3) URL rejected: Malformed input to a URL function

blocks.title: Why It Failed
items: Special characters like <highlight>< ? > ' </highlight> break URL parsing.
The failure occurs at the HTTP transport layer, not inside PHP.
Raw payloads can work only if properly URL-encoded.
To make transport safer and more reliable, Base64 encoding is used.

blocks.text: Convert the payload to Base64.
Transport Encoding Pitfalls

blocks.title: Why Base64 Sometimes Breaks
items: In URLs, <highlight>+</highlight> is interpreted as a space.
<highlight>&</highlight> splits query parameters.
<highlight>=</highlight> may interfere with parameter parsing.
<highlight>%</highlight> starts URL encoding sequences.
If Base64 contains +, /, or =, it must be URL-encoded before sending.
Always assume HTTP transport can mutate your payload.

blocks.text: File Writing Using data://
If direct output is not returned, use file writing for blind execution confirmation.
The file is written in the server's current working directory.
To confirm the working directory:
Verify File Content
Always URL-encode Base64 payloads before sending them via GET parameters. Reliable exploitation requires controlling every encoding layer.

Expect Wrapper - LFI

blocks.title: expect://
items: The <highlight>expect://</highlight> wrapper allows execution of system commands directly from PHP.
It does NOT require PHP tags like <highlight><?php ?>.</highlight>
It works only if the <highlight>PECL Expect extension</highlight> is installed and enabled.
If the wrapper is available, <highlight>include()</highlight> will execute OS commands.
This wrapper is rarely enabled in real-world production environments.

blocks.text: Execution Flow

blocks.title: How Command Execution Works
items: The application calls <highlight>include($_GET['file']);</highlight>
The <highlight>expect://</highlight> wrapper interprets the value as a system command.
The command executes on the operating system.
The output of the command is returned as stream content.
<highlight>include()</highlight> outputs the command result to the browser.

blocks.text: Basic command execution test.
Checking Wrapper Availability
If 'expect' appears in the output, the wrapper is enabled.
Lab Installation (Rarely Works on PHP 8+)

blocks.title: Important Notes
items: The expect extension is not installed by default.
It often fails to compile on modern PHP versions.
Most production servers do NOT enable this wrapper.
It is mainly seen in CTF environments.

blocks.text: Practical Value

blocks.title: Real-World Relevance
items: Impact: Immediate Remote Code Execution (RCE).
Difficulty: Very low if enabled.
Probability in production: Extremely low.
Not worth focusing heavily on for real-world bug bounty training.

PHAR Wrapper - LFI

blocks.title: phar://
items: The <highlight>phar://</highlight> wrapper allows access to PHP Archive (PHAR) files.
PHAR files can contain <highlight>serialized metadata</highlight>.
When accessed through certain file functions, PHP automatically performs <highlight>deserialization</highlight>.
If a vulnerable class contains <highlight>__wakeup()</highlight> or <highlight>__destruct()</highlight>, this can lead to <highlight>Remote Code Execution (RCE)</highlight>.
This wrapper is highly relevant in real-world applications with file upload functionality.

blocks.text: Execution Flow

blocks.title: How Deserialization Leads to RCE
items: The application allows <highlight>file upload</highlight> (e.g., image files).
An attacker creates a malicious <highlight>PHAR archive</highlight> disguised as an image (e.g., file.jpg).
The PHAR contains malicious <highlight>serialized object metadata</highlight>.
The application later calls <highlight>include($_GET['file']);</highlight> or another file function.
When accessed via <highlight>phar://</highlight>, PHP automatically deserializes the metadata.
If a gadget chain exists, <highlight>__destruct()</highlight> or <highlight>__wakeup()</highlight> executes attacker-controlled code.

blocks.text: Basic PHAR Access Test
Assume a file named image.jpg was uploaded.
If the file is a crafted PHAR, deserialization may trigger automatically.
Requirements for Exploitation

blocks.title: Conditions Needed
items: The server must allow <highlight>file uploads</highlight>.
The application must use a vulnerable file operation (include, require, file_exists, etc.).
A <highlight>deserialization gadget chain</highlight> must exist in the application.
The PHAR file must be reachable via the filesystem path.

blocks.text: Why phar:// Is Dangerous

blocks.title: Real-World Relevance
items: Used in real-world <highlight>WordPress</highlight> and <highlight>Laravel</highlight> vulnerabilities.
Works even when direct PHP code injection is blocked.
Does not require <?php ?> in the request.
Can bypass certain file extension restrictions.
Frequently appears in modern CVEs involving file handling.

blocks.text: Practical Value

blocks.title: Impact Assessment
items: Impact: High (Potential RCE via deserialization).
Difficulty: Medium to High (Requires gadget chain knowledge).
Probability in production: Moderate (file uploads are common).
High value wrapper for serious security research.

What is Log Poisoning?

Log Poisoning is a technique where an attacker injects malicious PHP code into a server log file and then uses a Local File Inclusion (LFI) vulnerability to include that log file, causing the injected code to execute.
This works because PHP parses any file included via <highlight>include()</highlight> or <highlight>require()</highlight> as PHP source code, regardless of its file extension.
Lab Setup
Environment Setup

Step 2 - Attempt to Read Access Log

blocks.text: Even though access.log had read permissions, the directory <highlight>/var/log/apache2</highlight> did not allow traversal by the web server user.
The directory had restricted execute permissions. To allow traversal for lab purposes:

Step 4 - Trigger Code Execution
Multiple Payload Execution
If the payload appears multiple times inside the log file, it executes multiple times because PHP parses the entire file and runs every <?php ?> block it encounters.
Why This Works

blocks.title: Execution Mechanism
items: include() reads the entire file, not line by line.
PHP parses the file regardless of its extension.
Text outside PHP tags is printed.
Code inside <?php ?> is executed.
Repeated payloads result in repeated execution.

blocks.text: Conclusion

Log Poisoning transforms an LFI vulnerability into Remote Code Execution by injecting PHP into writable logs and forcing the application to include them. The attack succeeds because the application blindly includes attacker-controlled content without validation.

What is Reflected XXE?
Reflected XXE occurs when a server parses attacker-controlled XML input and reflects expanded external entity content directly in the HTTP response.
Vulnerable PHP Code

blocks.code:
<?php
$xml = file_get_contents("php://input");

$dom = new DOMDocument();
$dom->loadXML($xml, LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD);

echo $dom->saveXML();
?>

blocks.text: <highlight>LIBXML_DTDLOAD</highlight> allows DOCTYPE processing. <highlight>LIBXML_NOENT</highlight> forces entity expansion. Without both, reflected XXE would not work.
Step 1 - Confirm XML Parsing
The server reflects the XML, confirming that user-supplied input is parsed and returned.
Step 2 - Define External Entity
Step 3 - Send Malicious XML
Step 4 - Observe Reflected File Content
The entity &xxe; is expanded by the XML parser, causing the contents of /etc/passwd to be injected into the XML response and reflected back to the attacker.
Execution Flow

blocks.title: How Reflected XXE Executes
items: User sends malicious XML with DOCTYPE.
Parser loads DTD (LIBXML_DTDLOAD).
Entity expansion is enabled (LIBXML_NOENT).
Parser encounters &xxe;.
SYSTEM resource is fetched.
Content replaces entity reference.
Application reflects processed XML.

blocks.text: Required Conditions

blocks.title: Conditions for Reflected XXE
items: Application must parse XML input.
DOCTYPE must be allowed.
Entity expansion must be enabled.
Response must reflect parsed XML to observe output.

blocks.text: Conclusion

Reflected XXE allows attackers to read local files when XML parsing is misconfigured. The vulnerability exists because unsafe parser flags enable external entity expansion and the application reflects the processed output.

blocks.title: XXE Practice Lab
blocks.text: Download the vulnerable PHP lab and payload collection.
What is Blind XXE?
Blind XXE occurs when the server parses attacker-controlled XML and expands external entities, but does NOT reflect the processed XML in the HTTP response.
Vulnerable PHP Code (Blind Scenario)

blocks.code:
<?php
$xml = file_get_contents("php://input");

$dom = new DOMDocument();
$dom->loadXML($xml, LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD);

echo "Processed";
?>

blocks.text: The XML is parsed with entity expansion enabled, but the processed XML is NOT returned. Therefore, entity output cannot be seen directly.
Step 1 - Setup Attacker Server
Step 2 - Create External DTD (evil.dtd)
%file reads and base64-encodes the target file. %evil dynamically creates a new entity that forces the server to send the file content to the attacker server.
Step 3 - Create Blind Payload
The payload loads the external DTD from the attacker. The DTD injects the exfil entity. The &exfil; reference triggers the outbound request.
Step 4 - Send Malicious XML
Step 5 - Observe Outbound Request
The victim first requests evil.dtd. Then it sends a second request containing base64-encoded file data as a query parameter.
Execution Flow

blocks.title: How Blind XXE Executes
items: User sends malicious XML.
Server parses DOCTYPE (LIBXML_DTDLOAD enabled).
External DTD is fetched from attacker.
Parameter entities are expanded.
Dynamic exfil entity is created.
XML body references &exfil;.
Server makes outbound HTTP request with file data.
Attacker receives exfiltrated content.

blocks.text: Required Conditions

blocks.title: Conditions for Blind XXE
items: Application must parse XML input.
DOCTYPE processing must be enabled.
External entity expansion must be allowed.
Outbound network requests must be permitted.
Attacker-controlled server must be reachable.

blocks.text: Why Base64 Encoding is Used
Raw file content may contain newlines and special characters that break the HTTP request. Base64 ensures safe transmission inside a URL.
Limitations

blocks.title: Common Practical Limitations
items: URI length restrictions (large files fail).
Outbound traffic filtering may block exfiltration.
Modern parsers often disable DTD processing by default.
WAF may block suspicious DOCTYPE usage.

blocks.text: Conclusion
Blind XXE allows attackers to extract sensitive data even when the application does not reflect parsed XML. Data exfiltration occurs through outbound requests triggered by entity expansion.
What is Billion Laughs Attack?
Billion Laughs is an XML Entity Expansion Denial of Service attack where nested entities recursively expand into exponentially large text, exhausting memory and CPU during XML parsing.
Root Cause

The attack works when the XML parser allows internal DTD processing and entity expansion (e.g., LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD). The parser recursively replaces entity references without strict expansion limits.
Vulnerable PHP Code

blocks.code:
<?php
libxml_use_internal_errors(true);

$xml = file_get_contents("php://input");

$dom = new DOMDocument();
$dom->loadXML($xml, LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD);

echo "Parsed successfully";
?>

blocks.text: LIBXML_DTDLOAD loads DTD definitions. LIBXML_NOENT forces entity expansion. Together they allow recursive entity substitution during parsing.
Classic Billion Laughs Payload

blocks.code:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
 <!ENTITY lol "lol">
 <!ENTITY lol1 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
 <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;">
 <!ENTITY lol3 "&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;">
 <!ENTITY lol4 "&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;">
 <!ENTITY lol5 "&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;">
 <!ENTITY lol6 "&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;">
 <!ENTITY lol7 "&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;">
 <!ENTITY lol8 "&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;">
 <!ENTITY lol9 "&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;">
]>
<root>&lol9;</root>

blocks.text: Exponential Growth Calculation
Base entity length = 3 bytes ('lol'). Each level multiplies by 10. Final size at level n = 3 × (10^n). At level 9 → 3 × 10^9 = 3,000,000,000 bytes (~3GB).
Internal Parser Execution Flow

blocks.title: How libxml Expands Entities
items: Parser reads DOCTYPE and builds entity table.
Entity definitions are stored in a hash map.
When &lol9; is encountered, recursive expansion begins.
Each entity is replaced by its defined value.
Replacement buffers are allocated on heap.
Nested replacements trigger further recursion.
Memory grows exponentially due to repeated string concatenation.
CPU usage spikes due to recursive decoding.

blocks.text: Memory and CPU Behavior
Each expansion requires new buffer allocation and copying of previous content. Intermediate buffers also consume memory. Actual usage exceeds theoretical final text size.
Observing Resource Exhaustion

blocks.code:
htop
# or
ps aux | grep php

blocks.text: During attack, PHP process shows high CPU utilization and rapid memory growth. On unprotected systems, this leads to memory exhaustion or OOM killer termination.
Safe Testing Strategy
Reduce depth (e.g., up to lol4 or lol5) or reduce multiplier (5 instead of 10). This prevents multi‑GB expansion and allows safe observation.
Modern libxml Protections

blocks.title: Built-in Defenses in libxml 2.11+
items: Entity expansion counter limit.
Maximum recursion depth restriction.
Maximum text node size limit.
Abort parsing on expansion overflow.
Internal loop detection.

blocks.text: Detecting Protection Trigger
Modern parsers may output errors like 'Entity expansion limit exceeded' or 'Detected an entity reference loop'.
Variants Beyond Classic Billion Laughs

blocks.title: Advanced DoS Variants
items: Quadratic Blowup (large base entity repeated many times).
Parameter Entity Bomb using %entities.
Hybrid XXE + DoS (external DTD + expansion).
Compression-style nested payloads.
Deep but narrow recursion chains.

blocks.text: Mitigation
Disable DTD processing and entity substitution. Avoid LIBXML_NOENT in production. Enforce strict memory limits at application level.
Conclusion

Billion Laughs is a parser-level Denial of Service attack exploiting recursive entity expansion. Modern parsers implement strict expansion limits, but legacy systems and custom parsers remain vulnerable.
What is XInclude?

<highlight>XInclude</highlight> is an <highlight>XML feature</highlight> that allows one XML document to include content from another file using <highlight><xi:include></highlight> elements. It is processed at the <highlight>XML parsing stage</highlight> and does not require a <highlight>DOCTYPE</highlight> declaration like classic <highlight>XXE</highlight>.
Root Cause

The vulnerability occurs when the <highlight>XML parser</highlight> has <highlight>XInclude processing enabled</highlight> (e.g., <highlight>DOMDocument->xinclude()</highlight>) and <highlight>user-controlled XML input</highlight> is parsed without validation. The parser fetches <highlight>external resources</highlight> referenced in the <highlight>xi:include</highlight> element.
Why XInclude Matters

blocks.title: Difference from Classic XXE
items: Does NOT require <highlight><!DOCTYPE></highlight>.
Works even when <highlight>DTD processing</highlight> is disabled.
Often bypasses <highlight>naive XXE protections</highlight>.
Requires explicit <highlight>XInclude processing call</highlight>.
Looks like normal XML structure (less suspicious).

blocks.text: Vulnerable PHP Code

The dangerous part is <highlight>$dom->xinclude()</highlight>. This explicitly tells <highlight>libxml</highlight> to process <highlight><xi:include></highlight> elements and fetch <highlight>external resources</highlight>.
Basic File Read Payload
The parser fetches <highlight>/etc/passwd</highlight> and inserts its content into the XML output. <highlight>parse="text"</highlight> forces raw text inclusion instead of XML parsing.
Internal Execution Flow

blocks.title: How XInclude Works Internally
items: Parser loads initial XML document.
Namespace <highlight>http://www.w3.org/2001/XInclude</highlight> is detected.
When <highlight>xinclude()</highlight> is called, <highlight>libxml</highlight> scans for <highlight><xi:include></highlight> nodes.
For each include node, libxml fetches the resource from <highlight>href</highlight>.
Resource is loaded into memory.
Content replaces the <highlight><xi:include></highlight> element in DOM tree.
Final DOM is serialized back to output.

blocks.text: XInclude for SSRF
If network access is allowed, the server makes a backend <highlight>HTTP request</highlight> to the internal service. This converts XInclude into an <highlight>SSRF primitive</highlight>.
Can XInclude Lead to RCE?

Direct <highlight>RCE</highlight> is rare. XInclude is primarily a <highlight>file read primitive</highlight> or <highlight>SSRF vector</highlight>. However, if included content is later passed to <highlight>eval()</highlight>, <highlight>include()</highlight>, or template rendering engines, it may escalate to code execution.
Detecting XInclude Vulnerability

If <highlight>DOCTYPE-based XXE</highlight> is blocked but XInclude works, you will see <highlight>external file content</highlight> reflected after adding <highlight>xmlns:xi</highlight> and <highlight>xi:include</highlight> elements.
Mitigation

blocks.code:
$dom->loadXML($xml, LIBXML_NONET | LIBXML_NOERROR | LIBXML_NOWARNING);
// DO NOT call $dom->xinclude();

blocks.text: Avoid calling <highlight>xinclude()</highlight>. Use <highlight>LIBXML_NONET</highlight> to block network access. Validate or sanitize XML input.
Conclusion

<highlight>XInclude</highlight> is an XML inclusion mechanism that can be abused for <highlight>file disclosure</highlight> and <highlight>SSRF</highlight> when <highlight>xinclude()</highlight> processing is enabled. It bypasses traditional <highlight>XXE defenses</highlight> because it does not rely on <highlight>DTD</highlight>.

title: Lab 1 - Reflected, Blind and XInclude XXE

blocks.title: XXE Challenge
blocks.text: Download the vulnerable PHP lab and payload collection.
XXE Full Exploitation Lab – Reflection, XInclude & Blind

This lab simulates a vulnerable XML processing service built with PHP and libxml. The application accepts XML input and parses it server-side. Your objective is to fully assess XML parsing behavior and determine whether the application is vulnerable to reflected XXE, XInclude injection, and blind (OOB) XXE.
Engagement Rules

blocks.title: Operational Constraints
items: Do NOT inspect or modify backend source code.
Do NOT access server files directly.
Only interact through HTTP requests.
Only submit XML payloads.
You may run your own listener for OOB testing.
Document proof for each vulnerability class.

blocks.text: Target Endpoint
If the XML structure is valid, the application returns processed node values. If parsing fails, it returns HTTP 400. Some parsed content may be reflected in the response.
Starting XML
Phase 1: XML Parsing Baseline
Submit valid and malformed XML to confirm parsing behavior. Determine which elements are reflected and how strict the structural validation is.
Phase 2: Internal Entity Expansion (Reflected XXE)
Introduce a DTD with a custom internal entity. Reference the entity inside a reflected node. If the entity value appears in the response, document the vulnerability and assess impact.
Phase 3: External Entity Resolution
Attempt to reference a local file using a SYSTEM entity. Determine whether file contents are reflected. Confirm whether external entity resolution is enabled.
Phase 4: XInclude Injection

Attempt to inject XInclude elements within accepted XML structure. Determine whether the parser processes XInclude directives. If successful, assess whether local file inclusion is possible via XInclude.
Phase 5: Blind XXE (Out-of-Band)
Assume reflection is disabled. Configure a local HTTP listener and attempt to trigger an outbound request via external DTD loading. Confirm blind XXE through observable callbacks.
Phase 6: File Exfiltration via OOB
Chain external DTD loading with file retrieval and outbound exfiltration. Extract the contents of runtime/secrets.dat using blind techniques. Provide decoded proof of exfiltrated data.
Technical Analysis Requirements

blocks.title: You Must Explain
items: Why entity expansion occurs.
How external DTD loading works in libxml.
Why XInclude may bypass DTD restrictions.
Why parameter entities are required for blind chaining.
What parser configuration is likely enabled.
How this vulnerability should be properly mitigated.

blocks.text: Final Objective
Demonstrate full-spectrum XXE exploitation: reflected, XInclude-based, and blind OOB exfiltration. Provide technical reasoning, proof of exploitation, and mitigation strategy.
